display_title: Missing critical references and lacking necessary FLOPs comparisons

content.title: Missing critical references and lacking necessary FLOPs comparisons
content.review:
The authors propose to decompose the standard convolutional layer into a 2D dictionary and the corresponding linear coefficients. By sharing the decomposed coefficients, the authors argue that cross-layer correlations can reside in such low rank formulation. The coefficient sharing also leads to model size reductions. The paper investigates the flexibility and compatibility of the proposed ACDC weight sharing mechanism by image classification and few-shot classification tasks.

The main weakness of the submission might be that there have been many studies on low-rank representation of the convolutional operation. However, the authors did not reference and discuss the fundamental related work [R1] that is one of the first few early works on exploring low-rank representation of convolution layers. Besides, the authors cited recent work (Kornblith et al., Morcos et al., and Raghu et al.) in the submission, but did not discuss the differences between the proposed atom-coefficient decomposition and other mentioned works, either in fundamental formulation aspect or practical performance aspect. The paper can be largely improved if the fundamental difference and performance gap (accuracy and efficiency) were shown.

While the paper shows clear model size reduction, in practice FLOPs might be equally if not more important when deploying edge friendly models. Models with less number of parameters do not necessarily translate to higher efficiency. It largely depends on how those parameters are wired as a whole. In the main experimental results (Table 2 and Table 3), the authors did not present FLOPs reduction. In table 4, the authors only show FLOPs comparisons with VGG16 and ResNet18, which are few years old and are known to be highly redundant networks. I suggest the authors clearly demonstrate the FLOPs reduction in Table 2 and Table 3 to strengthen the submission.

Again in the main experimental results (Table 2 and Table 3), the competing methods are a few years old such as SqueezeNet, ShuffleNet, MobileNet-V2, etc. It is important to compare the proposed weight sharing technique with more recent baselines such as MobileNet-V3 [R2] or EfficientNet [R3]. Although models found by architecture search algorithms can be orthogonal to manually designed decomposition approaches, it is important to understand the ballpark comparison with recent best performing efficient network architectures. 

[R1] Jaderberg et al. Speeding up Convolutional Neural Networks with Low Rank Expansions. In ECCV 2014.
[R2] Howard et al. Searching for MobileNetV3. In ICCV 2019.
[R3] Tan et al. EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks. In ICML 2019.

content.comment:
Thanks for pointing out the missing reference. 
As mentioned above, this paper proposes a theoretically motivated and justified, simply plug-and-playing placement to standard convolutions to explore and exploit the correlations in filters. 
Reducing computation, as a side product, is not the primary objective of this paper. 
And deployment on edge friendly model is not and will not be discussed in the paper.

content.title: ConvNet compression
content.review:
The paper explores a form of model compression that reduces the number of parameters and FLOPs for VGG/ResNet type models.
In isolation, the results look promising but there is a lack of comparison to related work.
Some relevant points of comparison would be:
1) Models using 'hand-designed' group or depthwise convolutions such as 
 a) ResNext, 2016
 b) MobileNet and EfficientNet, ICML 2019
2) Model compression methods like 
 a) ConDenseNet, CVPR 2018
 b) Stable Low-rank Tensor Decomposition for Compression of Convolutional Neural Network ECCV 2020
 c) And the Bit Goes Down: Revisiting the Quantization of Neural Networks, ICLR 2020
 d) TCNN: Towards Convolutional Neural Networks Compression via Global&Progressive Product Quantization, BMVC 2020

Comparing in terms of the number of parameters:
**Here** 5.77M parameters 72.22% top1, versus EfficientNet B0 5.3M parameters 77.1% top-1 accuracy
**Here** 16.37M parameters 75.96% top1, versus EfficientNet B3 12M parameters 81.6% top-1 accuracy
Table 3 does not give #FLOPs, but based on Table 4 I would guess the method uses five times more FLOPs than comparable EfficientNets.

Compared to other methods using compression to minimize model size: 
**Here** 72.22% top1 with 5.77M 32bit parameters vs TCNN: 77.55% top1 with 5.09MB of storage

Lastly, the name is a bit confusing. Is there suppposed to be any relationship to:
'ACDC: A Structured Efficient Linear Layer, https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05946'

content.title: Thanks for the comments.
content.comment:
- Thanks for pointing out the higher numbers. 

We introduce our method primarily as a new structural regularization to deep CNNs, by exploiting layer correlation in a CNN.
We consider directions like developing novel architectures with neural architecture search (e.g., EfficientNets) complementary to ours.
Therefore, providing the same level of parameter and FLOP reduction comparing to the best efficient network architectures is not the focus of this paper.
And all the methods we include to compare in Table 3 are end-to-end trained methods based on the same underlying networks ResNet34 and ResNet50. 


- Name of ACDC

The mentioned paper happens to adopt the same acronym as ours, but it is not closely related. We are happy the use of overlapping acronyms is limited to the filed and closely related contributions, otherwise the community couldn’t use, for example, the very popular CNN for concern of association with the news channel.

content.title: Reviews
content.review:
Summary:
  This paper proposed to use shared-weights crossing multiple layers to learn compact CNN models. This idea is similar to the structural learning for a CNN. The results show that the proposed achieves very high parameter efficiency.


Strong points:

  1. This paper proposed to learn a compact and shared weights to increase the parameter efficiency while achieving good results.
  2. This paper cooperates with dropout idea to regularize the network and achieves better results.


Weak points:

  1. The novelty from ACDC-group is limited due to the group convolution has shown the parameter efficiency in the prior art, e.g. ResNeXt.
  2. The comparison is somehow unclear and few heursitc baselines should be considered.
  3. Some important references are missed. 
    - "Learning Filter Basis for Convolutional Neural Network Compression" ICCV 2019
    - "Group Sparsity: The Hinge Between Filter Pruning and Decomposition for Network Compression", CVPR 2020
    - "Gate Decorator: Global Filter Pruning Method for Accelerating Deep Convolutional Neural Networks", NeurIPS 2019
    - "CondConv: Conditionally Parameterized Convolutions for Efficient Inference", NeurIPS 2019


Questions:

  1. How does the author handle a network with different kernel sizes? like in resnet has a 7x7 in the beginning and then 1x1 and 3x3 layers, under -net settings, do all layers share the same dictionary? 

  2. The author introduces drop-atom as a regularizer to further improve performance. From Fig. 6, it provides about 0.5% gain on cifar10. Deop-atom is like droppath/stochastic depth for a normal CNN. I think it will be fairer to apply similar techniques to the baseline for a more fair comparison.

  3. In Table 1, comparing to regular convolution is straightforward but since there are many known techniques to increase parameter utilization, like  (1) point-wise convolution + depthwise convolution (2) grouped convolution + channel shuffle. Those should be the baseline to compare.

  4. In Table 2, why the authors' method is all based on WRN? to more fair compare to others, using the same/similar backbone will be more clear to see the advantage of the proposed approach as authors claim the ACDC is plug and play.

  5. How does this approach saving runtime? Is it proportional to the FLOPs reduction? I expected the speed will be slower because there are additional steps to construct kernels from atoms. but is this overhead significant?


Others:

  1. The author mentioned the results of cifar10/cifar100 are the mean of five runs, in such cases, it will be better to show the variance of those runs as well.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thanks for the comments.
content.comment:
- Kernel sizes

Yes, as shown in Figure 1 and Equation (1), the kernel size of a filter in our method is only decided by the atoms, which are layer-specific, thus the cross-layer coefficient sharing allow different kernel sizes in each layer. 


- Atom drop

Atom drop will not result in droppath/stochastic depth. A convolutional filter in ACDC is reconstructed by multiplying the layer specific atoms with the shared coefficients, dropping atoms leads to `under-represented’ convolutional kernels. This is a unique regularization enabled only by our method that does not equal to any existing regularizations.


- Comparisons

Note that our method are plug-and-play replacements to standard convolutions only. We present Table 1 for self-comparison purpose, which demonstrates the significant flexibility of deploying this method based on actual real-world scenarios.
In fact, the comparisons you suggested can already **all** be found in Table 2 (first block), where MobileNet (point-wise convolution + depthwise convolution), shufflenet (channel shuffle) and NASNet (neural architecture search) are all included in this currently reviewed version.
In Table 2, the main objective is to show that our method can achieve comparable or even better performance comparing to other **plug-and-play** methods (second block). Since most of the methods in the second block adopt WRN as the underlying network, we used the same architectures and tried to find the configurations that have similar parameter scales comparing to those compared methods. The advantages of our method are thus demonstrated by higher accuracy and slightly lower parameters at each scale. E.g., comparing to SWRN 28-10-2, WRN-28-10 ACDC-block m24 achieves higher accuracies with 3.8M fewer parameters.

- FLOPs

Saving computation is not our primary focus. Though, as we show in Table 4, enabling sharing with grouping can save computation. And we observe that the additional kernel reconstruction does not influence the run time noticeably.

display_title: Interesting way of sharing parameters, but the method seems a bit too complex and with many hyper-parameters for real use

content.title: Interesting way of sharing parameters, but the method seems a bit too complex and with many hyper-parameters for real use
content.review:
This paper introduces a new factorization of a convolutinal neural network (CNN) learning parameters. A convolutional layer is decomposed in a 2D dictionary of spatial-only filters plus a channel recombination layer. Dictionaries among different layers are shared among the entire network or among blocks. This acts like a regularization that reduces the number of CNN parameters and helps reduce overfitting.
Experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet with different network configurations show that the propose method is quite competitive in terms of parameter reduction and performance.

Quality & Clarity:
The presentation of the approach can be improved. For instance, in the introduction it seems that canonical correlation analysis is used in the approach, while after reading the rest, I understood that it was used just for motivation. Also illustrations could be improved. For instance Fig. 4 is too small.

Originality & Significance:
Sharing weights in CNN is not new. Authors should consider methods based on weights clustering such as ("Deep k-Means: Re-Training and Parameter Sharing with Harder Cluster Assignments for Compressing Deep Convolutions", 2018) and ("Clustering Convolutional Kernels to CompressDeep Neural Networks", ECCV18). 

Pros:
- The way of sharing weights seems new and leads to good results.
- Fig. 5 shows that for few-shot learning reducing the number of parameters is important to obtain better performance on larger networks.

Cons:
-  The way of sharing weights introduces additional hyper-parameters that should be defined and makes the method more difficult to be used in practice.
- Instead of presenting results with all the different configurations of the method, it would have been easier to select the best setting form table 1 and then compare with the state of the art on only that setting.
- With many different configurations it is difficult to fully understand which trade-off between accuracy and compression would be achieved
- Table 4 shows the computational cost of different configurations, but without the corresponding accuracy it is not very useful for understanding the real capability of the method to reduce the computational cost of a model. Also, it is not clear if the number of flops in the table would translate in a real speed-up.

Additional comments:
- The decomposition in 2D convolutions seems to me similar to depth-wise convolution (Chollet et al. 2017). Authors should at least acknowledge those similarities in related work. 
- The use of symbols is a bit confusing: in Fig.1 "x" is used for DA matrix multiplication, while in fig. 2 the matrix multiplication is represented with another symbol and in the equations as normally it is represented without any symbol.
- The reduction of overfitting can produce also a model that is more robust to noise. Could the authors evaluate that?
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thanks for the comments.
content.comment:
- Thank you for your suggestions.

Instead of proposing a new network architecture, the proposed plug-and-play framework offers a flexible way of reparametrizing deep CNNs motivated by observed layer correlations in a CNN. 
As a plug-and-play method, our method allows a wide range of design trade-offs, supporting various real-world scenarios based on factors such as dataset scale and training resources. Such large flexibility is a clear advantage, as it allows various degrees of structural regularization without touching the original architecture, further obtaining improved results, especially when supervision is insufficient as shown in our few-shot experiments. Such flexibility is enabled by only two additional hyperparameters, the number of atoms and atom drop rate, with the second one being optional. The influence of both hyperparameters to the network performance are all evaluated in the paper. We believe those two easily chosen hyperparameters will not hurt the practical usage of our method. 

- Computation

The same or similar architectures in Table 4 can all be found in Table 1.

- Depth-wise convolution

Thanks for pointing out the missing discussion on the similarity to depth-wise convolution. Although they happen to share similar implementation, the proposed framework originated from atom decomposition of convolutional filters.

content.title: Paper contributions
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for the valuable feedbacks and pointing out the missing reference. 
We want to highlight again that this is not at all a paper on network compression or efficient architectures, we instead explore and exploit the underlying correspondence and correlations among convolutional layers within a CNN. Specifically, hinted by the observed correlations among layers under proper channel alignments, we decompose the convolutional kernels among layers, and enforce shared composition coefficients within sub-structures of a CNN. This reparametrization of convolutional kernels significantly reduce the network redundancy while maintaining performance. 

Furthermore, it also enables fast model adaptation and better interpretability of CNNs.

Variants of the proposed method based on channel shuffle can further reduce computation.

Being theoretically motivated and justified, simply plug-and-playing our method directly to modern network architectures can achieve high performance and also network compression (as a by product), comparable to many modern heavily tailored light-weight networks. However, as a paper investigating and exploiting the underlying correlation and redundancy of CNNs, compressing models and reducing FLOPs are not our primary objective, are just a consequence of the careful analysis.

The proposed ACDC are direct plug-and-play replacements to standard convolutions, therefore all the experiments we performed are based on networks with standard convolutions. 

Finally, we consider directions such as neural architecture search [3], post processing methods to deep networks [1,2,5,6,7], and heavily tailored efficient network structures [4] complementary to our efforts.

[1] Stable Low-rank Tensor Decomposition for Compression of Convolutional Neural Network, ECCV 2020
[2] And the Bit Goes Down: Revisiting the Quantization of Neural Networks, ICLR 2020
[3] Searching for MobileNetV3, ICCV 2019.
[4] EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks, ICML 2019.
[5] Learning Filter Basis for Convolutional Neural Network Compression, ICCV 2019
[6] Deep k-Means: Re-Training and Parameter Sharing with Harder Cluster Assignments for Compressing Deep Convolutions, ICML 2018
[7] Clustering Convolutional Kernels to CompressDeep Neural Networks, ECCV 2018
